# Mexican-Origin Adolescent Mothers’ Economic Contexts, Educational Re-Engagement, and their Children’s School Readiness

**Authors:** Elana R. McDermott; Laudan B. Jahromi; Adriana J. Umaña-Taylor; Stefanie Martinez-Fuentes; Shandra M. Jones; Kimberly A. Updegraff

**Affiliations:** Harvard Graduate School of Education | Teachers College Columbia University | Arizona State University

## Abstract

Drawing on data from a longitudinal study of 204 Mexican-origin adolescent mothers, their mother figures, and their children, the current investigation examined (a) adolescent mothers’ educational re-engagement and attainment beginning during their pregnancy and ending when their child was five years old; and (b) the influence of the family economic context on adolescent mothers’ educational re-engagement and attainment and their children’s academic and social-emotional outcomes. Findings detailed adolescent mothers’ re-engagement in school after the birth of their child and showed that family income during adolescents’ pregnancies was directly associated with re-engagement and attainment, and also initiated cascade effects that shaped adolescents’ economic contexts, their subsequent re-engagement and attainment, and ultimately their children’s academic and social-emotional outcomes at age 5.

The family economic context is a critical influence on parenting practices, experiences of stress, and sources of support that benefit children’s academic achievement (e.g., Contreras et al., 2002). Among Latinx adolescent mothers, the family economic contexts shapes not only adolescents’ economic and educational outcomes but may extend across generations to shape the educational outcomes of their children. For example, Latinx adolescent mothers who come from higher socioeconomic family contexts may have access to interpersonal and material investments (e.g., assistance with child care, financial resources) that reduce their experiences of economic hardship, help them to stay on track to graduation from high school, vocational school, and/or college. In turn, when Latinx adolescent mothers re-engage in their education after the birth of their child, this educational re-engagement and attainment may support children’s school readiness by allowing adolescent mothers to accrue greater resources, reduce economic stress, and inform their parenting practices in ways that promote their children’s school readiness (Contreras et al., 2002). As such, not only are the consequences of family economic context apparent in the educational outcomes of Latinx adolescent mothers, but through these direct and indirect pathways, the family economic context shapes their access to resources and experiences of stress that informs their children’s academic readiness through the preschool years (Cabrera et al., 2019). In other words, the family economic context initiates a developmental cascade of direct and indirect consequences (Masten & Cicchetti, 2010), that links socioeconomic status, family interaction processes, and child development cumulatively across generations.

The current investigation examined educational re-engagement among Mexican-origin adolescent mothers from their pregnancies through the first five years immediately following the birth of their children. We specifically examine the associations between family economic context during pregnancy (operationalized as family income) and Mexican-origin adolescent mothers’ experiences of economic hardship during their children’s first year of life. Not only are the first years of adolescent motherhood a critical period in shaping adolescent mothers’ economic and educational trajectories (Oxford, Lee, & Lohr, 2010), but it is also a time when many families experience new economic challenges and learn to navigate parenting. Moreover, this period co-occurs during critical developmental periods for adolescents and their children, during which time young mothers are establishing patterns of interactions with their infants that serve as the basis for the cognitive, linguistic, and social-emotional experiences that children need for positive development, particularly in the context of adversity (Blair & Raver, 2012; Cabrera et al., 2019). As such, we examine how the family economic context shapes adolescent mothers’ educational re-engagement and attainment during the first five years of motherhood (Barr & Simons, 2012; Black, Polidano, & Tseng, 2012; Hurst, Kelly, & Princiotta, 2004; McDermott, Anderson, & Zaff, 2018) and, in turn, their children’s academic and social-emotional outcomes at age five (Mollborn & Dennis, 2012; Tang et al., 2016).

A focus on Mexican-origin adolescent mothers is warranted, given that Mexican-origin adolescents have the highest adolescent birthrates in the U.S. (Ventura, Mathews, Hamilton, Sutton, & Abma, 2011) and have a lower likelihood of attaining an educational credential (e.g., high school diploma or GED) than their non-parenting peers (Manlove & Lantos, 2018). Not only are adolescents who are pregnant or parenting likely to leave school (e.g., Porche, Fortuna, Lin & Allegria, et al., 2011), they also have lower rates of re-engagement in educational pursuits after dropout than individuals who leave school for other reasons (Entwisle, Alexander, & Olson, 2004). These lower levels of educational attainment are negatively associated with health, employment, and financial outcomes throughout the life course (e.g., McDermott, Donlan, & Zaff, 2019). Among Mexican-origin adolescents, these outcomes may be exacerbated by the economic and social challenges they face, including language barriers, discrimination, school segregation, and low-wage work, that contribute to their disproportionately high rates of poverty compared to other ethnic-racial groups (Cabrera et al., 2019; Edwards, 2019). Given that mothers’ educational attainment may confer economic, health, and social benefits to themselves, their children, and society (e.g., McDermott, 2018; Tang et al., 2016), understanding Mexican-origin adolescent mothers’ re-engagement and degree attainment and how it is shaped by and informs the intergenerational transmission of economic and educational inequality is important.

## Educational Re-engagement among Mexican-origin Adolescent Mothers

Educational re-engagement and degree attainment is a heterogeneous process (McDermott, Donlan, & Zaff, 2019) – with individuals’ returns to school encompassing different numbers of attempts, varying success rates, and different educational levels at which individuals re-engage (e.g., high school diploma, vocational school). Although returning to school is common among early school leavers (Hurst et al., 2004), among Latinx adolescent mothers, nearly half do not obtain a high school diploma or GED (Manlove & Lantos, 2018). This low level of educational attainment may be due to systemic barriers to returning to school related to adolescent pregnancy and parenting, including limited access to childcare, the demands of parenting (e.g., work demands, family responsibilities; SmithBattle, 2007), schools that are not flexible to their needs, and transportation issues – all of which may be exacerbated by the discrimination and marginalization they face as girls and women of color (Hines-Datiri, 2017).

The economic context may create distinct barriers to re-engagement as Latinx adolescent mothers may be particularly vulnerable to economic hardship (e.g., Tang et al., 2016) – with Latinx adolescents frequently citing the need to work to support their families as their main reason for early school leaving (Pew Research Center, 2009). Barriers to re-engagement may partially explain why, despite similar educational aspirations, adolescent mothers from minoritized ethno-racial groups are less likely to report that they expect to attend college or achieve a college degree than their non-parenting peers (Barr & Simons, 2012). Moreover, many of these barriers occur in the years immediately following school leaving, while Latinx adolescent mothers are navigating parenting infants and young children. Research has shown that the years immediately after leaving school are crucial to educational re-engagement and attainment – with the highest rates of re-engagement occurring within five years of leaving school (Black et al., 2012). When adolescent mothers do re-engage, those who complete a high school credential by age 19 are more likely to pursue education beyond high school or attend college (Oxford et al., 2010), educational attainment that may provide benefits to Latinx adolescent mothers and to their children (e.g., Hendrick & Maslowsky, 2019).

## Economic and Educational Opportunity across Generations

Prior theory and research examining the intergenerational transmission of poverty and education among Mexican-origin families (Altschul, 2012) suggests multiple pathways by which the economic context shapes the developmental outcomes of subsequent generations. Prior research has demonstrated support for the idea that economic context both exacerbates family stressors (i.e., family stress model) and informs parents’ access to resources that are associated with children’s positive developmental outcomes (i.e., family investment model; Conger & Donnellan, 2007), creating important links between family socioeconomic factors, family processes, and adolescents’ educational outcomes (Altschul, 2012). Concerns about the negative impact of economic stress on educational and psychosocial outcomes among Mexican-origin adolescent mothers are particularly relevant, given higher rates of poverty among this population in the U.S. (Edwards, 2019), and that the intergenerational effects of parents’ economic hardship on their children’s educational attainment is stronger among individuals from low-income households (Wightman & Danziger, 2014), with those who experience economic adversity earlier in their lives more likely to experience economic hardship in adulthood compared to those who do not (Oxford et al., 2010).

In line with this theoretical foundation, family economic context is associated with adolescent mothers’ developmental outcomes, in part, by shaping their own economic circumstances. Specifically, research has shown that economic factors are central to Latinx adolescents’ decisions to leave school, and that family financial constraints serve as a barrier to further education (e.g., Gonzalez, Stein, Shannonhouse, & Prinstein, 2012). Economic instability within the family, due to illness, household disruption, and family caretaking responsibilities may place additional stress on adolescents (Minnis et al., 2013), and create barriers to re-engagement. It is possible that economic strain may not only push Latinx adolescent mothers out of educational pursuits, but that continued economic hardship may prevent them from re-engaging given the competing demands of work, school, and parenting. However, research has also shown that the constrained economic opportunities associated with not having a high school diploma or GED may motivate individuals to return to school (Black et al., 2012; McDermott et al., 2018) and that adolescent mothers, in particular, may be motivated to return to school by their desire to be economically stable and independent (Hines-Datiri, 2017; SmithBattle, 2007). Even so, compared to individuals from more economically disadvantaged backgrounds, those from more advantaged socioeconomic backgrounds are more likely to re-engage (Entwisle et al., 2004; Hurst et al., 2004) and, among adolescent parents, higher aspirations for a college degree are associated with increased re-engagement (Barr & Simons, 2012). Higher socioeconomic status positively predicts degree attainment among adolescent parents by age 26 (Mollborn, 2010), possibly because greater economic resources can be drawn on to help adolescent mothers navigate educational barriers and keep their education on track (SmithBattle, 2007).

## Adolescent Mothers’ Educational Re-engagement and Children’s School Readiness

Whether and how adolescent mothers return to school may also shape their children’s outcomes because these educational gains may provide mothers with greater access to financial resources, human capital (e.g., skills for gathering information), cultural capital (e.g., behaviors valued in educational spaces), and social capital (e.g., network connections; Harding, Morris, & Hughes, 2015) that are relevant to children’s school readiness. Children’s school readiness refers to their acquisition of the foundational skills associated with success in elementary learning environments. These skills may include pre-academic capacities (e.g., early math and literacy skills) as well as social-emotional competencies that support learning, such as self-regulation (e.g., Blair & Raver, 2015). Self-regulation refers to the ability to modulate one’s mental and behavioral responses, and includes subcomponents such as executive function (i.e., cognitive or mental forms of self-regulation that involve flexible, goal-directed thinking) and delay of gratification (i.e., the capacity to regulate one’s behaviors in order to wait for a desirable outcome; Blair & Diamond, 2008). Prior research has shown that the social-emotional skills of Latinx children are similar to those of their peers from other ethnic-racial groups; however, there are notable disparities in their pre-academic capacities, with maternal education consistently related to Latinx children’s cognitive development (see Cabrera et al., 2019 for a review). Furthermore, research has shown that across ethnic-racial groups the children of adolescent mothers may be at particular risk for developmental delays in social-emotional and cognitive development leading to inadequate school readiness (e.g., Mollborn & Dennis, 2012; Tang et al., 2016).

Research drawing on nationally representative samples including Latinx families has shown that increases in maternal education and higher socioeconomic resources among adolescent mothers are associated with their children’s higher developmental functioning (Mollborn & Dennis, 2012) and greater likelihood of being ready for school in terms of early math and reading achievement (Tang et al., 2016). Increases in adult mothers’ education when their children were between 24 and 36 months were associated with increases in children’s expressive and receptive language skills (Magnuson, Sexton, Davis-Kean, & Huston, 2009). It is likely that increases in maternal education lead to greater economic resources that allow Latinx families to invest greater time and financial resources into children’s learning, and that promote their cognitive development (Cabrera et al., 2019). Indeed, prior research among adult mothers has shown that increases in educational attainment are related to greater income and lower levels of unemployment and poverty-related risk (Pressler, Raver, & Masucci, 2016), that mothers who re-engage in educational pursuits increase their engagement with their children’s schools (Crosnoe & Kalil, 2010), and that increases in maternal education are positively associated with children’s cognitive scores (Harding, 2015).

In line with the notion that intergenerational transmission may operate through skills-based, behavioral, and social pathways (Harding et al., 2015), research has shown that Latinx adolescent mothers’ economic resources are associated with their children’s cognitive development and social-emotional and behavioral outcomes (Cabrera et al., 2019; Mollborn & Dennis, 2012; Tang et al., 2016), including the development of self-regulatory processes that are important to their academic success. Family processes related to the socioeconomic status of Mexican-origin families may foster both barriers to and supports for their children’s academic achievement (Altschul, 2012; Cabrera et al., 2019). For example, Mexican-origin parents with higher education may earn greater income, may have more time to be involved with, and may feel more efficacious in helping their children with schoolwork than those with lower education and economic resources, translating into positive academic outcomes for their children (Bhargava, Bámaca-Colbert, Witherspoon, Pomerantz, & Robins, 2017). Additional research has shown that the relation between socioeconomic status and Latinx children’s pre-academic skills is mediated by home learning environments, investments, and enrichment activities (Cabrera et al., 2019; Hackman, Gallop, Evans, & Farah, 2015), suggesting an interdependence between family characteristics, their socioeconomic contexts, and children’s school readiness.

Although prior research has focused predominantly on intergenerational transmission from parent to child, a growing body of research supports the idea that children’s educational outcomes are also directly informed by their grandparents’ resources (e.g., Anderson, Sheppard, & Monden, 2018; Møllegaard & Jæger, 2015). Given the timing of their pregnancies during the life course, it is likely that adolescent mothers cohabitate with and/or are financially dependent on their parents during their children’s early life. As such, adolescent mothers’ family economic context (i.e., their parents’ economic context) may directly inform their children’s educational outcomes. Moreover, living in three-generation households is common among Latinx families (Cohn & Passel, 2018), and may function as a cultural asset that promotes children’s positive developmental outcomes (Pilkauskas, 2014). Indeed, prior research has shown that co-residence across three generations was associated with children’s greater school readiness (i.e., more expressive language) among Latinx families compared to those who did not live in three generation households (Pilkauskas, 2014). Grandparents’ economic context may buffer the effects of experiences that are detrimental to education across generations by reducing the stress associated with poverty through additional economic support (Møllegaard & Jæger, 2015).

## Current Investigation

The current investigation examined educational re-engagement and attainment in a sample of Mexican-origin adolescent mothers, their families, and their children. First, we explored their educational re-engagement and attainment including the timing of their returns, the number of times they were enrolled in school, and their educational attainment over the course of six years, beginning during their pregnancy and ending when their child was five years of age. In doing so, we provide a more complete description of educational re-engagement and attainment among Latinx adolescent mothers. Second, drawing on theoretical perspectives on the intergenerational transmission of capital (e.g., Harding et al., 2015), we examined the associations between family economic context (i.e., income) and Mexican-origin adolescent mothers’ experiences of economic hardship, educational re-engagement and attainment across their children’s first five years of life, and their children’s school readiness outcomes at age five. With our focus on children’s pre-academic development, we chose to examine children’s outcomes when children in the study were approximately five years of age and entering kindergarten. This five-year period also aligns with the window of time that has been identified in prior research as critical to re-engagement. In these confirmatory models, we hypothesized that lower family income during the third trimester of Latinx adolescent mothers’ pregnancies would be related to higher experiences of economic hardship during the first year of their children’s lives. In turn, we hypothesized that greater economic hardship would be related to lower levels of educational re-engagement and attainment across the first five years of their children’s lives. Finally, we hypothesized that higher levels of educational re-engagement and attainment would be positively related to children’s academic readiness, delay of gratification, and executive function, in line with research showing the benefits of additional maternal education to children’s academic readiness and self-regulation (Mollborn & Dennis, 2012; Tang et al., 2016). Given the multitude of pathways through which family income may shape child development, we did not anticipate that economic hardship and educational re-engagement and attainment would fully mediate the association between family income and children’s outcomes. Rather, we hypothesized that greater family income during adolescents’ pregnancies would be directly related to children’s greater academic readiness and self-regulation at age five, operationalized as children’s academic readiness, delay of gratification, and executive function (Jahromi, 2017). Additional exploratory analyses were requested via the review process and are presented in the Sensitivity Analyses section.

## Method

### Participants

Data came from a six-wave longitudinal study of 204 Mexican-origin families and included mother figures (e.g., a biological mother or aunt), adolescent mothers, and their children (author citation). Data were collected when adolescent mothers were in their third trimester of pregnancy (Wave 1; W1), and when children were 10 months of age (W2), 2 years of age (W3), 3 years of age (W4), 4 years of age (W5), and 5 years of age (W6). The current study included data from adolescent mothers’ reports at all waves, mother figures’ reports at W1, and assessments of children’s outcomes at W6.

Retention rates for adolescent mothers were 96% at W2, 85% at W3, 84% at W4, 85% at W5, and 84% at W6. Attrition analyses comparing adolescents who participated at all six waves (n = 143) versus those who did not (n = 61) revealed no significant differences in demographic variables at W1 including adolescents’ nativity, χ2(1) = 0.003, p = .96; adolescents’ age, t(202) = .98, p = .33; adolescents’ perceived economic hardship, t(201) = –0.05, p = .96; mother figures’ highest level of education t(201) = .10, p = .92; or family income, t(196) = .87, p = .39. For mother figures, retention rates were 91% at W2, 82% at W3, 81% at W4, 84% at W5, and 82% at W6. Attrition analyses comparing mother figures who participated at all six waves (n = 133) versus those who did not (n = 71) revealed a significant difference at W1 in mother figures’ nativity, such that a higher percent of foreign-born mother figures participated in all six waves (68.7%) compared to U.S.-born mothers (53.8%), χ2(1) = 3.72, p = .05. There were no other differences in demographic variables at W1 including mother figures’ age, t(202) = .56, p = .58; mother figures’ highest level of education t(201) = −1.26, p = .21; or family income t(196) = .71, p = .48.

At W1, adolescent mothers’ average age was 16.80 years (SD = 1.00), and mother figures were, on average, 40.75 years of age (SD = 6.93). At W6, children’s average age was 60.41 months (SD = .50). A majority of adolescent mothers were U.S.-born (64%), whereas the majority of mother figures were born in Mexico (68.1%). Slightly more than half of the children in the study were male (58%). At W1 mother figures had an average of 9.00 years of schooling (SD = 3.37). At W1, 86.8% of adolescent mothers were co-residing with their mother figure, and 67% were co-residing at W2.

### Procedure

Pregnant adolescents were recruited from community agencies, health centers, and high schools in a Southwestern metropolitan area. To be eligible for the study, participants had to be of Mexican descent, 15 to 18 years of age, in their third trimester of pregnancy, not legally married, and had to have a mother figure who was also willing to participate. Parental consent and youth assent were obtained for participants younger than 18 years old; for all others, informed consent was obtained.

Data were collected via face-to-face in-home interviews, lasting about 2.5 hours, and conducted by bilingual student and staff research assistants. Questions were read aloud by research assistants and recorded on paper surveys. Translation procedures described in Knight, Roosa, and Umaña-Taylor (2009) were followed for all data collected in Spanish, such that measures were translated, then back translated, and discrepancies were reviewed by a bilingual team of translators. A native Spanish speaker of Mexican origin reviewed the final Spanish version of all items. Most adolescent mothers completed the interview in English at W1 (61.3%), whereas most mother figures completed the interview in Spanish (69.1%). Child assessments were conducted in each child’s dominant language, indicated by the adolescent mother. Participant incentives were $25 at W1, $30 at W2, $35 at W3, $40 at W4, $50 at W5, and $60 at W6. Adolescent mothers received an additional $25 for the child’s participation at each wave. All procedures were approved by the university’s human subjects review board.

### Measures

#### Re-engagement (W1 to W6).

Responses to two questions were used to examine re-engagement: whether adolescents were in school (i.e., yes; no, dropped out; no - graduated or earned a GED) and their highest level of education at each wave (i.e.., coded based on the number of years of school completed from 1= 1 year to 20 = Doctorate or Advanced degree). Across the six waves, these variables were used to determine whether the participant had returned to school at any wave, the first wave they returned to school, the number of waves they reported being in school, and their educational attainment at W6. Next, we used these variables to create a continuous variable representing both adolescent mothers’ return to schooling and their educational attainment (0 = did not re-engage; 1 = re-engaged, did not complete a high school degree; 2 = re-engaged, earned a high school diploma or GED; 3 = re-engaged, some vocational school, some college, or a bachelor’s degree).

#### Family Income (W1).

Four items were summed to calculate the annual family income at W1, as reported by mother figures: the total amount of public assistance, total amount of food stamps, the total personal wages, and income from any other household members over the last year. At W1, family income ranged from $94 to $114,000 (M = 27,323.73, SD = 19,893.30).

#### Adolescent Economic Hardship (W2).

Adolescents’ reports of economic hardship at W2 were assessed using the 17-item Economic Hardship measure (Barrera, Caples, & Tein, 2001). This scale assesses four components of economic hardship. The financial strain subscale (two items; e.g., “In the next three months, how often do you think that you will experience bad times such as poor housing or not having enough food?”) asked adolescents to indicate how often in the next 3 months their family is likely to be without food, housing, or basic necessities. Responses were rated on a 5-point Likert scale from almost never (1) to almost always (5). The inability to make ends meet subscale (two items; e.g., “Think back over the last 3 months and tell me how much difficulty you had with paying your bills”) assessed the degree to which adolescents had difficulties making ends meet and was rated on a 5-point Likert scale from no difficulty at all (1) to a great deal of difficulty (5). The not enough money for necessities subscale (four items; e.g., “I had enough money to afford the kind of car we need”) assessed the degree to which adolescents perceived their ability to afford necessities. Responses were rated on a 5-point Likert scale from strongly disagree (1) to strongly agree (5). The nine-item economic adjustments subscale asked adolescents to respond to questions about adjustments or cutbacks their family has had to make (e.g., “In the last 3 months, has your family had to shut down the heat or air conditioning to save money even though it made the house uncomfortable?”). Adolescents responded either yes (1) or no (2). Scoring guidelines from Barrera et al., (2001) were followed, whereby a composite score was created by standardizing each subscale score, weighting them based on the number of items within each subscale, and creating a mean with the scores. Higher scores reflected greater perceived economic hardship. A reliability alpha coefficient is not appropriate for this variable because scores are weighted, and some are dichotomous response scales. Correlations between standardized subscale measures were all significant at the p < .001 level and ranged from .42 to .62.

#### Academic Readiness (W6).

The Woodcock Johnson III Tests of Achievement (WJ-III; Woodcock, McGrew, & Mather, 2000) and the Batería III Woodcock-Muñoz (Batería-III; Muñoz-Sandoval, Woodcock, McGrew, and Mather, 2005) were used to assess academic readiness for children whose primary language was English (69.8% of children at W6) or Spanish (30.2% of children at W6). We chose to examine children’s outcomes at W6 because that timepoint is when children averaged five years of age and were entering kindergarten. We use a mean score of four subtests that assess children’s early literacy and math skills: 1) Letter-Word Identification (Identificación de letras y palabras), which asked children to identify letters that appear in large type on the test book; 2) Applied Problems (Problemas aplicados), which asked children to analyze and solve simple math problems; 3) Passage Comprehension (Comprensión de textos), which assessed children’s ability to match a pictograph representation of a word or phrase to an actual picture of an object; and 4) Picture Vocabulary (Vocabulario sobre dibujos), which measured oral language development and lexical (word) knowledge as children identify pictured objects. The child’s raw score (i.e., sum of correct responses) was converted to a standardized score using the WJ-III Compuscore program.

#### Executive Function (W6).

At W6, executive function was measured using the Dimension Change Card Sort-Advanced (DCCS), which is designed to assess the core abilities associated with problem representation, planning, rule execution, and evaluation (Zelazo, 2006). Children were shown two model cards (e.g., a red rabbit and a blue boat). Then they were given cards that differed from the model cards in one dimension (e.g., red boats and blue rabbits) and were asked to sort the cards according to specific rules about a particular dimension. Children completed a total of 24 trials in three phases: pre-switch, post-switch, and borders. To begin the six pre-switch trials, children were told they would play the “shape game,” and were instructed to place cards with rabbits inside the bin with the red rabbit model card, and cards with boats inside the bin with the blue boat model card. Next, for six post-switch trials, children were told that they would play a new game, the “color game,” and would no longer be playing the “shape game.” In the “color game,” they were instructed to place red cards inside the bin with the red rabbit model card, and blue cards inside the bin with the blue boat model card. Finally, children participated in 12 border trials, in line with the advanced version of the DCCS (which is best suited for children who are approximately five years old). Cards varying in shape and color were presented with or without black borders around the card. Children were instructed to play the “color game” if there was a black border around the card, and to play the “shape game” if there was no border around the card. Children were given one practice round for the borders trials.

The percentage of correct trials within each set of trials (i.e., pre-switch, post-switch, and borders trials) was coded. In line with the criteria set forth by Zelazo (2006) 5 out of 6 correct post-switch trials and 9 out of 12 correct borders trials constituted a pass. An overall score was created as follows: we assigned a score of 0 if children failed the pre-switch phase; assigned a score of 1 if they passed the pre-switch (shape) phase but failed the post-switch (color) phase; assigned a score of 2 if they passed both the pre- and post-switch phases (shape and color) but failed the second post-switch phase (border); assigned a score of 3 if they passed all three phases (M = 1.36, SD = .74).

#### Delay of Gratification (W6).

Children’s delay of gratification at W6 was measured using the gift bag task (Kochanska, Coy, & Murray, 2001). After the child had completed all of the activities for the home visit, and while the adolescent was in another room of the home, the experimenter entered the room and announced, “Guess what? This is a present for you!” The experimenter placed a gift bag containing tissue paper and a small gift in front of the child. The tissue paper prevented the child from seeing the gift inside the bag, and the child was not expecting a gift. Once the child turned his or her attention to the gift, the experimenter said, “But I want you to open the present with your mom. Wait here while I go to get her. Try not to touch it until I come back with your mom, OK?” The experimenter then left the room for three minutes. Children’s behaviors during the three-minute wait were video recorded and coded. After three minutes, the experimenter returned with the child’s mother and allowed the child to open the gift bag. Children’s responses were coded as follows, 1 = child pulls gift from the bag; 2 = child puts hand into the bag; 3 = child opens the bag to peek inside; 4 = child touches the bag without peeking; 5 = child neither touches nor peeks into the bag. Higher scores reflect greater delay on the part of the child (M = 3.95, SD = 1.04).

#### Covariates.

Covariates included adolescents’ age at W1 and in which language children completed the WJ-III or Batería-III (1= WJ-III/English, 2 = Batería-III/Spanish), as this indicates the language they used to complete all assessments.

## Results

### Educational Re-engagement

We examined descriptive statistics to identify patterns of educational re-engagement among adolescent mothers, including the timing of their first re-engagement, the number of times they returned to school (i.e., the number of waves and which waves they reported being in school), and their educational attainment over the course of six years of study. These exploratory analyses revealed that at W1, more than half of the adolescent mothers (58.3%; n = 119) were in school, 36.8% (n = 75) reported that they had dropped out of school (i.e., before W1), and nearly 5% (n = 10) had graduated from high school or earned a GED before W1. Across the six years of study, approximately two-thirds (66.3%; n = 134) of the adolescent mothers reported returning to school at any wave after W1. Among these 134 mothers who re-engaged, a majority (76.9%) reported being in school again at W2 (i.e., when their children were 10 months of age), with the remaining 23.1% re-engaging at later time points; there was considerable variability in the number of times and the waves at which they returned (see Table 1).

This re-engagement resulted in varying levels of educational attainment among the adolescent mothers at W6. Table 2 reports adolescent mothers’ educational attainment at W6, wave of first re-engagement, and the number of times they reported being in school across the waves of study by their educational attainment at the end of the study. Of the 68 mothers who did not re-engage, 86.8% had less than a high school degree at W6 (13.2% had a degree at W1). In addition, there were 27 adolescent mothers who re-engaged at some point over the six waves of study and reported less than a high school education at W6. Their enrollment at subsequent waves highlights that, although this group of mothers persisted in returning to school year after year, they had not attained a high school credential five years after the birth of their child. There were also 55 mothers who re-engaged and reported having obtained a high school diploma or GED credential. A majority (64.1%) of these mothers returned for the first time in the year after their child’s birth (i.e., at W2) and reported being in school at only one subsequent wave (60.9%). An additional 20.3% of mothers who obtained a high school credential reported being in school at two subsequent waves and a small group (4.7%) reported being in school at three or more waves, suggesting that adolescent mothers had varying pathways to high school completion. Finally, 50 mothers re-engaged and completed vocational school, some college, or a college degree, with a majority (88%) returning for the first time in the year after their child’s birth (W2). Among these mothers, 16% were in school at only one additional wave, suggesting that these adolescent mothers may have completed a high school credential between waves or that they enrolled immediately in vocational training or college courses. In addition, 36% of those who completed vocational school or some college and beyond were in school at two additional waves, and 48% were in school at three or more waves. Lastly, of the 10 adolescent mothers who had obtained a high school credential prior to W1, only one returned to school in the subsequent waves.

### Adolescent Mothers’ Economic Contexts, Academic Re-engagement, and Child Outcomes

A path model conducted using Mplus examined the association between adolescent mothers’ economic contexts and their educational re-engagement and attainment and whether, in turn, their re-engagement and attainment was related to their children’s academic readiness, delay of gratification, and executive function. Table 3 presents descriptive statistics for the variables included in this analysis. Acceptable model fit was determined based on a non-statistically significant chi-square, the root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA) below .06 with an upper limit of .07, a standardized root square mean residual (SRMR) of less than .08, and a comparative fit index (CFI) and Tucker–Lewis index (TLI) above .90 (Hu & Bentler, 1999). Missing data were estimated using Full Information Maximum Likelihood (Muthén, Muthén, & Asparouhov, 2016).

We hypothesized that adolescent mothers’ economic contexts would relate to their children’s academic readiness, delay of gratification, and executive function via the following sequential mediation process. First, family income during adolescents’ pregnancy (W1) was expected to be related to adolescents’ economic hardship a year later (W2). Next, we hypothesized that economic hardship would be associated with adolescents’ educational re-engagement and attainment, and in turn, to their children’s outcomes. In addition, we expected that there would be a direct relation between family income at W1 and children’s outcomes at W6, given prior research showing direct relations between grandparent characteristics and children’s academic outcomes (e.g., Anderson et al., 2018).

#### Tests of hypothesized paths.

Given the potential for qualitative differences in the experiences and trajectories of adolescent mothers who had already completed their education at W1, the hypothesized model only included adolescents who had not completed a high school diploma or GED at W1 (n = 194). Results for the hypothesized model indicated acceptable fit, χ2(6) = 9.46, p > .05; CFI = .96; TLI = .84; SRMR = .04; RMSEA = .06 (90% C.I.: .00-.12). As shown in Figure 1, confirmatory findings revealed that there was a negative relation between family income at W1 and adolescent economic hardship at W2 such that higher family income during the adolescents’ pregnancies was related to lower economic hardship after the birth of their children. In turn, higher economic hardship among adolescent mothers at W2 (during the first year of their children’s lives) was related to lower educational re-engagement and attainment across the study. Put differently, mother figures’ economic context during the adolescents’ pregnancies were associated with adolescent mothers’ economic contexts during the first year of their children’s lives and, in turn, whether they re-engaged in and attained further education during the first five years of their children’s lives. In turn, adolescents’ re-engagement and attainment was positively related to their children’s W6 academic readiness and delay of gratification but was not related to their executive function at age five. There was a direct relation between family income at W1 and children’s executive function at W6 such that higher levels of family income during the adolescents’ pregnancies were related to higher executive function among their children at age five. Bias-corrected bootstrapping with confidence intervals were used to examine the indirect effects (Taylor, MacKinnon, & Tein, 2008). Findings indicated there were no statistically significant indirect effects for the relations between family income and children’s outcomes, between adolescents’ economic hardship and children’s outcomes, or between family income and adolescents’ educational re-engagement and attainment.

### Sensitivity Analyses

During the review process several contextual, educational, and sociodemographic variables were suggested as potential covariates or moderators that could be used to evaluate the robustness of these findings via exploratory analyses. Sociodemographic factors included adolescent mothers’ and mother figures’ nativity status, adolescent-mother figure co-residency, adolescent mothers’ and mother figures’ relationship status, and whether children attended daycare and the type(s) of childcare or preschool children attended. Next, prior measures of child outcome variables were examined as covariates. A final set of analyses examined educational and contextual factors (measured at W1). These analyses included adolescent mothers’ and mother figures’ education, adolescent mothers’ and mother figures’ educational utility, adolescents’ academic motivation, and adolescent mothers’ dating partner supports as covariates.

#### Sociodemographic factors.

Additional models testing sociodemographic factors included adolescent-mother figure co-residency, adolescent mothers’ and mother figures’ relationship status, children’s daycare attendance, and type of daycare (e.g., care by a family member at home, Head Start) as covariates, as well as multigroup models using adolescent mothers’ and mother figures’ nativity status as the grouping variable. Adolescent mothers’ relationship status at W1 was significantly related to adolescent mothers’ educational re-engagement and attainment, but these models demonstrated relatively poor fit. All other analyses revealed that there were no group differences and that these covariates were not significantly related to the mediators or outcomes of interest. Further, models indicated relatively poor fit when these factors were included. As such, these grouping variables and covariates were not retained in the model but were examined via post hoc tests. Post hoc analyses revealed that there were statistically significant differences in family income at W1 based on nativity, such that foreign-born adolescent mothers’ and their mother figures’ household incomes were lower than their U.S.-born counterparts, respectively (adolescent mothers: Mexico-born M = 23,564.34, SD = 14,368.49, U.S.-born M = 29,379.64, SD = 22,128.12, F(1, 196) = 3.92, p = .05; Mother figures: foreign-born M = 24,482.25, SD = 16,079.42, U.S.-born M = 33,859.12, SD = 25,665.23, F(1, 196) = 9.70, p < .01). In addition, there were statistically significant differences in whether adolescent mothers re-engaged based on their co-residency with their mother figures at W2 only, χ2(1) = 4.49, p = .03, with 72.1% of adolescent mothers who co-resided at W2 re-engaging over the course of the study compared to 56.7% of their counterparts who did not co-reside with their mother figures at W2. In other words, a greater percent of adolescent mothers who co-resided at W2 re-engaged over the course of the study compared to those who did not co-reside at W2. Results further indicated that adolescent mothers’ relationship status at W1 was related to their degree attainment and re-engagement as a covariate (β = .17, SD = .08, p = .03). Post-hoc tests revealed that adolescents who were in a relationship but not living together had higher re-engagement and degree attainment (M = 1.80, SD = 1.17) than those who were living with a partner (M = 1.29, SD = 1.18), F(4, 139) = 3.40, p = .05.

#### Prior child outcome measures.

An additional model examined the inclusion of prior wave measures of the three child outcomes. For academic readiness, the Woodcock Johnson was administered at W5 and W6. In contrast, the measures for delay of gratification and for executive function varied across the two waves of measurement so that children experienced different activities at each wave. At W5 delay of gratification was measured using a giftwrap task and executive function was measured using the Day/Night task (a test of inhibitory control). The model that examined these measures as covariates suggested that after accounting for earlier levels of academic readiness, delay of gratification, and executive function, adolescent mothers’ re-engagement and attainment was positively associated with children’s delay of gratification and academic readiness. In this model, the direct relation between family income and children’s executive function was not statistically significant. However, this model demonstrated poor model fit χ2(16) = 32.60, p < .01; CFI = .91; TLI = .78; SRMR = .08; RMSEA = .07 (90% C.I.: .04-.11). Given the relatively poor model fit, and that there was only one substantive change to the model, we did not include these variables as covariates.

#### Educational and contextual factors.

Additional models showed that adolescent mothers’ academic motivation at W1 and mother figures’ education at W1 were statistically significantly related to adolescent mothers’ educational re-engagement and attainment, but these models demonstrated relatively poor fit. As such, these covariates were not retained in the model, but were examined via post hoc tests to better understand potential differences in adolescent mothers’ educational re-engagement and attainment. Specifically, when included as a covariate, adolescent mothers’ academic motivation at W1 was positively related to their educational re-engagement and attainment (β = .26, SD = .11, p = .02), but not their children’s outcomes. Additional post-hoc tests showed that adolescent mothers who re-engaged (M = 3.37, SD = .42) had higher academic motivation at W1 than those who did not re-engage (M = 3.21, SD = .57), F(1, 182) = 4.23, p = .04 and those who achieved a high school degree or GED had higher academic motivation at W1 than those who did not obtain a high school credential (Mdiff = .20), F(2, 180) = 3.34, p = .04. In addition, mother figures’ education at W1 was positively related to adolescents’ educational re-engagement and attainment (β = .09, SD = .04, p = .01), but not their children’s outcomes. Its inclusion demonstrated relatively poor model fit. Additional post-hoc tests did not show significant differences in mother figure education among adolescent mothers who re-engaged (M = 9.26, SD = 3.43) compared to those who did not re-engage (M = 8.50, SD = 3.24), F(1, 189) = 2.06, p = .15.

Lastly, adolescent mothers’ level of education at W1 was examined as a covariate. Although the hypothesized model excluded adolescent mothers who had achieved a high school diploma or GED at W1, the inclusion of these educational differences as a covariate accounted for qualitative differences in education at W1. As such, models were examined that included the full sample of adolescent mothers (N = 204). Results showed that adolescent mothers’ education at W1 was positively and significantly related to their later re-engagement and attainment (β = .26, SD = .08, p < .01) and negatively related to their children’s executive function (β = −.35, SD = .18, p < .05), but was not related to children’s delay of gratification or academic readiness. Post-hoc tests showed that there were no differences in education levels at W1 for adolescents who re-engaged (M = 9.52, SD = 1.29) compared to those who did not re-engage (M = 9.70, SD = 1.29), F(1, 99) = .38, p = .54, but there were differences in adolescents’ levels of educational attainment at the end of the study based on their education level at W1 (less than a high school education M = 9.08, SD = 1.36; high school diploma or GED M = 10.61, SD = 1.41; vocational school, some college or more (M = 10.00, SD = 1.00), F(2, 99) = 12.36, p < .01. In other words, adolescent mothers who had higher levels of education during their pregnancy also tended to have higher levels of education when their children were five. In contrast to all previous tests of robustness, the inclusion of adolescent mothers’ education at W1 as a covariate demonstrated good model fit, χ2(7) = 8.51, p > .05; CFI = .99; TLI = .94; SRMR = .03; RMSEA = .02 (90% C.I.: .00-.10). As a result of this exploratory process, we include this covariate in the final model (Figure 1). There were no substantive changes to the relations of interest. As previously described, findings showed that higher family income during adolescents’ pregnancy was associated with adolescent mothers’ own economic contexts, which in turn were related to whether they re-engaged in and attained further education. Adolescents’ re-engagement and attainment was related to greater academic readiness and delay of gratification for their children, but not to their executive function. Higher family income at W1 was related to higher executive function among children. In addition, this revised model showed a statistically significant indirect relation from adolescent mothers’ education at W1 to children’s academic readiness at W6 via adolescent mothers’ educational re-engagement and attainment (β = .05, SE = .03, p = .05, C.I.: .11, 72). There were no other statistically significant indirect effects.

## Discussion

Despite the importance of further educational attainment to adolescent mothers’ and their children’s life outcomes (Crosnoe & Kalil, 2010; Harding, 2015; Mollborn & Dennis, 2012; Tang et al., 2016), little research examines Latinx adolescent mothers’ re-engagement in educational pursuits (e.g., SmithBattle, 2007). The current investigation expands the literature by describing the educational re-engagement and attainment of Mexican-origin adolescent mothers and adds to research examining the interrelations between economic context, family processes, and educational outcomes among Mexican-origin families (Altschul, 2012). Findings suggest that educational re-engagement and attainment is a common, but heterogeneous, process among Mexican-origin adolescent mothers. Spanning from pregnancy through the first five years of their children’s lives, these findings add to the literature by detailing when, how many times, and at what levels of education Mexican-origin adolescent mothers re-engaged in educational opportunities – with yearly assessments capturing important developmental periods during infancy and early childhood, as well as the years immediately after school leaving, which are critical to educational re-engagement (Black et al., 2012; Hurst et al., 2004). Moreover, we find support for the idea that family economic context initiates a development cascade that shapes adolescent mothers’ and their children’s educational outcomes. Specifically, Latinx adolescent mothers who came from higher socioeconomic family contexts tended to report less economic hardship, which in turn was related to greater educational re-engagement and attainment during the first five years of their children’s lives. Moreover, findings suggest that the consequences of family economic context during adolescent mothers’ pregnancies informs their children’s educational outcomes, demonstrating associations with children’s academic readiness via increases to adolescent mothers’ educational re-engagement and attainment and a direct association with children’s later executive function.

In complement to research showing that motherhood may inspire adolescents’ renewed interest in and commitment to their education (SmithBattle, 2007), these findings demonstrate the primacy of returning to schooling quickly after the birth of their child for many Mexican-origin adolescent mothers and aligned with prior research showing the value that Latinx families place on education (Pew Research Center, 2009). However, the number of subsequent waves the mothers were enrolled in school suggest that Mexican-origin adolescent mothers encounter educational barriers. Specifically, the variation in adolescent mothers’ enrollment statuses prior to giving birth to their children, the timing of their return to schooling, and the types of educational opportunities they pursued illuminated important differences in re-engagement. For example, there was a small group of mothers who returned to school but were unable to attain a high school degree or degree equivalent. Among them, five mothers reported being in school at two or three waves after the birth of their child – meaning that although this group of mothers persisted in pursuing educational opportunities, they had not successfully completed a high school credential five years after the birth of their child. In contrast, slightly more than half of those who re-engaged did so at only one wave and were able to attain a high school credential (i.e., diploma or GED), and/or enrolled directly in college or vocational school. These findings highlight the heterogeneity that exists in Latinx adolescent mothers’ re-engagement (Colón, 2019) and suggest that educational persistence among Mexican-origin adolescent mothers encompasses a wide variety of pathways in and out of schooling.

Importantly, post-hoc analyses also suggested that there were relatively few systematic differences between mothers who re-engaged and those who did not in terms of contextual, educational, and sociodemographic variables (i.e., academic motivation, relationship status). Rather, those who re-engaged and attained subsequent educational credentials tended to be those who came from higher socioeconomic backgrounds, in line with prior research (Entwisle et al., 2004). That there were few differences in this model based on personal characteristics (e.g., nativity status) suggests that Mexican-origin adolescent mothers as a group may face similar systemic barriers to educational re-engagement and attainment. Prior research has noted that the barriers to completing high school among Mexican-origin adolescents include economic disadvantage (Pew Research Center, 2009) and linguistic discrimination and negative ideologies about Spanish at school (Murillo & Schall, 2016). Further research on the particular barriers that Mexican-origin adolescent mothers face in returning to school as well as the cultural strengths that may foster their educational re-engagement and attainment is needed.

The current investigation reiterates the importance of educational re-engagement and attainment in the transmission of economic and educational inequality across generations among Mexican-origin families (Altschul, 2012). Aligned with prior research and theory showing that economic contexts inform the educational trajectories and opportunities of subsequent generations (e.g., Entwisle et al., 2004), we found two differential pathways by which economic contexts relate to academic outcomes within the families of Mexican-origin adolescent mothers. First, the cascading effect of lower family income via its associations with greater economic hardship and, in turn, adolescent mothers’ lower rates of re-engagement and attainment, which in turn informed their children’s delay of gratification and academic readiness. These findings align with prior research suggesting a link between socioeconomic status and educational re-engagement (Hurst et al., 2004) and attainment among Latinx families (Pew Research Center, 2009), and re-iterate the importance of continued educational opportunities for Latinx adolescent mothers as a mechanism for supporting their children’s school readiness (e.g., Mollborn & Dennis, 2012; Tang et al., 2016). Second, findings from the current investigation showed that children’s executive function was directly related to their family economic context from before they were born, with children born into higher income families having higher executive function at age five than their lower family income counterparts. This finding aligns with prior research showing that poverty is a risk factor for the development of children’s executive function (e.g., Raver, Blair, & Willoughby, 2013) and the effects of poverty on Latinx children’s social-emotional and pre-academic development more broadly (Cabrera et al., 2019). This combination of direct and indirect longitudinal associations aligns with the idea that the family economic context initiates a developmental cascade that links socioeconomic status, family processes, and child outcomes across generations (e.g., Cabrera et al., 2019). Yet, the current investigation is not able to examine the micro-level processes that inform these associations. Prior research on Mexican American families has demonstrated support for both family investment models and family stress models in providing mechanisms by which family economic context may inform adolescents’ educational outcomes (Altschul, 2012). Given the importance of early childhood to the development of school readiness skills (Jahromi, 2017), further research that examines the differential mechanisms by which the prenatal family economic context and increased maternal education may inform children’s development is needed.

Aligned with prior theoretical work examining the determinants of parenting among Latinx adolescent mothers (Contreras et al., 2002), findings from the current investigation support the idea that economic context plays an integral role not only in Mexican-origin adolescent mothers’ re-engagement and attainment, but also in their children’s academic readiness. Positioning the family economic context as fostering a developmental cascade with cumulative effects across generations also highlights the importance of structural interventions aimed at mitigating its impact. Wide-ranging social policy that includes universal access to high-quality early childcare and universal basic income may remove barriers to educational re-engagement and attainment, support educational attainment, reduce stress during this period, enhance access to resources, and provide benefits to children’s school readiness (e.g., Hackman et al., 2015) and later development. Not only has prior research demonstrated positive effects for universal programs (e.g., universal prekindergarten, universal basic income; Blair & Raver, 2016; Ruckert, Huynh, & Labonte, 2018) – alleviating economic constraints may be particularly effective among Latinx adolescents more broadly, given research showing they are likely to report having left school to support their families (Pew Research Center, 2009).

In combination with these structural policy changes, programs aimed at promoting the educational outcomes of Mexican-origin adolescent mothers may include more flexible school arrangements, greater access to alternative pathways to degree completion for adolescent mothers, and culturally relevant targets for intervention. Information about how Mexican-origin adolescent mothers return to school and how these pathways may vary based on individual and structural characteristics is essential for designing the interventions aimed at fostering the developmental outcomes of adolescent mothers and their children. For example, findings suggest that the level of education that Latinx adolescent mothers have at the time of their pregnancy may be critical to understanding their future educational opportunities and trajectories. It is possible that Latinx adolescent mothers who have higher education levels are more likely to attain further educational credentials because they are encouraged to pursue alternative credentials (i.e., the GED), or because they have fewer years of schooling left to complete a degree, increasing their likelihood of finishing. Yet, prior theoretical work also highlights that resources that support or enhance Latinx adolescent mothers’ goals for their own development may conflict with the goals they have in their role as a parent (Contreras et al., 2002). Understanding the pathways that adolescent mothers take toward degree completion, including whether and how the developmental timing of their pregnancies impacts these trajectories, how adolescent mothers navigate potential conflicts between parenting and pursuing further education, and how school policies and programs (e.g., completing curricula online, alternative educational programs) may ease or hinder their return to educational contexts in relation to these goals will be crucial to designing effective interventions that promote their educational attainment and economic well-being. In addition, prior research has shown that high levels of communication with and academic support from mothers, romantic partners, and educators may promote positive academic outcomes among Mexican-origin students (Alfaro, Weimer, & Castillo, 2018). Incorporating these aspects into program design may further the effectiveness of these interventions among this population.

### Limitations

Although the current investigation advances the understanding of educational re-engagement and attainment among Latinx adolescent mothers, there are notable limitations. First, our measures asked adolescent mothers about their educational involvement at yearly intervals. Given that re-engagement may be marked by multiple attempts and disruptions in educational attainment, it is possible that adolescent mothers may have returned to schooling between waves but were out of school at the time of data collection. In addition, the requirement of a GED or high school diploma to attend college varies across states and institutions, and there are a variety of pathways for vocational school and college entrance. In the current investigation, it is not possible to determine whether participants pursued vocational training as a part of their high school curriculum, enrolled in adult high school programs at a college, passed college entrance exams without a high school credential, enrolled in non-degree credits, or undertook degree coursework at colleges without obtaining a high school credential. Future research that includes shorter time scales or asks adolescent mothers to reflect on their re-engagement in the time since they were last interviewed may illuminate understandings of how and why Latinx adolescent mothers re-engage.

The current investigation is also limited in that although we demonstrate that re-engagement and attainment is a mechanism by which family economic context is associated with children’s outcomes, we do not examine the process by which adolescent mothers’ educational re-engagement and attainment may be related to their educational and psychosocial outcomes and those of their children. For example, economic stressors and social supports may shape specific parenting processes among Latinx adolescent mothers (Contreras et al., 2002), which in turn may mediate the associations between re-engagement and attainment and child outcomes. Future research on the micro-level interactions that support these findings is needed. Relatedly, the current investigation does not account for potential changes in family economic context or adolescent mothers’ perceptions of economic hardship. Research that examines these changes in relation to differences in institutional access (e.g., high school programs for adolescent mothers; high quality early childcare) may provide greater insights into how institutional resources are accessed, and how they may better support the needs of Latinx adolescent mothers and their children. In other words, research that models the dynamic relations between economic context, institutional access, educational re-engagement, and child development is needed.

In addition, this study is unable to comment on the specific barriers that Latinx adolescent mothers encountered that may have informed this process. Future research that draws on mixed-method approaches is needed to elucidate structural, personal, and familial barriers to re-engagement. Although we were specifically concerned with the re-engagement of Mexican-origin adolescent mothers, this study does not offer a comparative sample of non-adolescent mothers to understand how economic context may inform their children’s development. Given that prior research has shown that children of adolescent mothers do not reach academic parity with those of non-adolescent mothers (Tang et al., 2016), further research is needed to investigate these models in other family contexts. Finally, our study focused on the role of income in the reproduction of economic and educational inequality across generations. However, there are additional forms of capital not measured by the present study (e.g., knowledge of educational systems; bilingual development) that may foster Latinx adolescent mothers’ re-engagement and may impact additional components of children’s academic and social-emotional outcomes not measured in the present study. Future research that examines these multiple forms of capital in tandem is needed to better understand the mechanisms by which income shapes the educational outcomes of Latinx adolescent mothers and their children.

### Conclusions

Educational re-engagement and attainment can have long-term benefits to adolescent mothers’ and their children’s physical health, and their psychosocial and financial well-being (e.g., Tang et al., 2016). Findings from the current investigation expand the research literature to examine re-engagement among Mexican-origin adolescent mothers and demonstrate how educational re-engagement and attainment is shaped by the economic context. In doing so, this study builds on a body of work that examines the transmission of economic and educational inequality across generations among Mexican-origin families. Furthermore, findings from the current investigation suggest that interventions that work to re-engage Latinx adolescent mothers in educational pursuits shortly after the birth of their child, that address the unique barriers Latinx adolescent mothers face in returning to school, and that alleviate structural economic and educational inequities may be particularly effective at creating intergenerational change.
